title: When does 100 become 200?
hook: Money grows 8% a year. How long until it doubles?

doesNotKnow: how a compound growth rate links to doubling time

misconception: At 8% a year money doubles in 100 / 8 = 12.5 years, as if only the original amount earned (simple-interest thinking).
objective: The learner can explain that compounding makes growth earn growth, so doubling comes sooner than 100 / rate, and can estimate the doubling time as 72 / rate (about 9 years at 8%).

claims.text: At 8% a year compounded yearly, money doubles in about 9 years: 1.08^9 = 1.999.
claims.source: 1.08^9 = 1.99900; exact doubling time ln 2 / ln 1.08 = 9.006 years. Recomputed with node.

claims.text: With simple interest at 8%, where only the first 100 earns, doubling takes 100 / 8 = 12.5 years.
The exact doubling time at rate r compounded yearly is ln 2 / ln(1 + r); the stage plots 100 (1 + r)^t year by year.

72 / rate gives 9 at 8% and is within about 0.2 years of the exact doubling time for every whole-number rate from 5% to 20%; the reveal also quotes 72 / rate against the exact time (ln 2 / ln(1 + r)) at the other rate the learner set, e.g. 8.0 vs 8.0 years at 9%.
claims.source: Tabulated in node for whole rates 2..20%: abs(72/r - ln2/ln(1+r)) = 1.00 (2%), 0.55 (3%), 0.33 (4%), then at most 0.20 for 5% to 20% (0.19 at 5%, 0.20 at 20%).

claims.text: 72 divides evenly by many whole rates (2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 9, 12), which is one reason the rule uses 72.
claims.source: Divisors of 72: 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 9, 12, 18, 24, 36, 72. The other reason (72 is close to 100 × ln 2 ≈ 69.3, nudged up for typical rates) was removed from the learner text in v3 as beyond the boundary; see Wikipedia 'Rule of 72' and Brealey, Myers & Allen, Principles of Corporate Finance.

recall.question: A fund grows 6% a year, compounded. Roughly how long does it take to double?
recall.why: 72 / 6 = 12 (exact: 11.9 years). Simple-interest thinking gives 100 / 6, about 17, which ignores growth on growth.
